extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in Serbian politics, higher education policy, and academic integrity
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style account documenting the timeline, institutional responses, and controversies around an academic plagiarism scandal (Siniša Mali), including legal, procedural, and policy changes in higher education. Focus is on describing events, institutional rules, reforms, and reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public availability of doctoral dissertations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Law on High Education was changed in 2014, with added obligation for doctoral dissertations to be publicly available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement was introduced as part of reforms aimed at transparency in doctoral work and is cited in relation to the Mali scandal.

rubrics_metrics.name: University plagiarism and doctoral study codes
rubrics_metrics.description: In July 2016 new codes were adopted at the university which regulate doctoral studies and plagiarism, as well as a new ethical code of the university.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These codes formalize procedures for handling suspected plagiarism; defenders raised retroactivity concerns, but the article notes plagiarism was already forbidden under former ethical codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: No statute of limitation for plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Rector Popović stated there is no statute of limitation for plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implies universities may investigate and sanction alleged plagiarism regardless of how long ago the degree was awarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-plagiarism procedures and technology
rubrics_metrics.description: In January 2020 the university adopted the 4th version of the anti-plagiarism code, acquired further anti-plagiarism software (like iThenticate), and committed to publicly announcing all decisions to increase transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officials expected simplified procedures and a rise in the number of reports; demonstrates an institutional rubric of using software and openness to detect and deter plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions for plagiarism (including automated termination)
rubrics_metrics.description: On 19 February 2020 the Senate amended the code to add an automated termination of employment as the clear consequence of plagiarism; previously the sanction included only stripping of the academic title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Change was prompted by specific cases (e.g., Aleksandar Jakšić); subsequent legal and administrative interventions (e.g., Labor Inspection ordering rehiring) show sanctions can be contested on formal/legal grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics commission complaint timeline (60 days)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon receiving a complaint, the faculty's ethics commission has 60 days to submit its opinion to the dean, who can then accept or reject it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies procedural timing expectations for internal complaints about non-academic behaviour and plagiarism; used in the FON complaint process described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court review limited to technical/procedural aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: Complaints to the Administrative Court concern only technical and procedural aspects of the plagiarism-review process and have no effect on postponing the university's substantive decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professors and commentators argued such court complaints are unlikely to overturn substantive academic findings; lack of judicial precedent makes outcomes uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immunity for commission members for views/votes
rubrics_metrics.description: The university added a clause to the Ethics Code stating that members of commissions cannot be liable for the views they express or the way they voted during plagiarism procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rector framed this as empowering independence and impartiality; critics said the clause shields those implicated and weakens accountability and ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-plagiarism software not sole basis for disputing doctorate
rubrics_metrics.description: The FON commission stated that 'software is not the basis for disputing Siniša Mali's doctorate' (Softver nije osnov za osporavanje doktorata Siniše Malog).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals a rubric that automated similarity/screening tools alone do not constitute definitive proof—human review and other evidence remain necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold for plagiarism / 'you can't plagiarize a little'
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic community statements such as 'you can't plagiarize a little' and reports quantifying portions of copying (e.g., one third, claims of 93% similarity) reflect expectations about unacceptable levels of copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community norms treat even limited copying as unacceptable; numeric percentages are used as indicators but the qualitative judgment remains important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal indexing based on faculty ethical status
rubrics_metrics.description: The Center for Education and Evaluation in Science (CEES) dropped FON's journals from SCIndeks in May 2019, citing the faculty's 'compromised ethical status' and many works published in predatory journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexing bodies may evaluate faculties/journals based on ethical behaviour, publication practices, and links to predatory publishing; loss of indexation is a reputational and evaluative sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accreditation body independence requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: ENQA placed the membership of the National Entity for Accreditation and Quality Assurance in Higher Education of Serbia (NAT) under supervision and later reduced NAT's membership because it remained under government influence rather than being independent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Independence of accreditation agencies from governmental/political control is treated as a standard; failure can lead to supervision/demotion with implications for recognition of qualifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural fairness and multi-agency oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple oversight mechanisms (university ethics boards, administrative courts, labor inspection, prosecution offices) can intervene in plagiarism cases, sometimes assessing different aspects (procedural legality vs. reputational damage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the Jakšić case where the Faculty fired him, the Administrative Court found procedural issues, and the Labor Inspection ordered rehiring—showing that procedural fairness and overlapping jurisdictions affect outcomes.
